problem: Encrypting every federated model weight can dominate clients’ compute time and upstream communication.
contribution: EncCluster encrypts a small codebook of weight centroids and encodes their positions with Binary Fuse filters before secure aggregation.
reading_guide: Separate accuracy loss, upstream bytes, and client encryption time; efficiency results do not establish protection against every inference attack.

diagram.title: Compress values, encode positions, aggregate securely
diagram.description: Each client splits clustered weights into centroids and mappings, encrypts the former and encodes the latter, then the server reconstructs encrypted weights and returns their aggregate.

stages.title: Train and cluster
stages.detail: Train locally, then split model weights into a small centroid set and a position mapping.

stages.title: Protect two components
stages.detail: Encrypt centroids; independently encode mappings with Binary Fuse filters.

stages.title: Reconstruct encrypted weights
stages.detail: Query the filters using shared seeds, then substitute encrypted centroids at the recovered positions.

stages.title: Aggregate and return
stages.detail: Combine partial keys to decrypt the weighted aggregate and return the global model.

diagram.footnote: The cycle returns the aggregate to clients. This preprint uses an honest-but-curious setup authority; filter encoding is distinct from cryptographic encryption.

results.title: Less encryption work and upstream traffic
results.question: What does clustering save relative to encrypting full updates?
results.context: CIFAR-10, ResNet-20, 30 clients, full participation, 128 clusters, 256-bit key. IID uses Dir(10); non-IID uses Dir(0.1). Accuracy changes are percentage points versus FedAvg; upstream ratios and seconds are lower-is-better.

source.label: Table 3, CIFAR-10 with full participation · PDF page 12

results.interpretation: EncCluster sends 28.4% of FedAvg’s upstream volume in this comparison, with 2.04 seconds of reported client encryption time and less than one percentage point of accuracy loss.
results.caveat: FedAvg + clustering is an unencrypted compression reference. The table provides one communication/time column across the two splits, no uncertainty, and no end-to-end training or server-cost measurement.

results.title: Accuracy across four architectures
results.question: Do the reported accuracy and encryption costs depend strongly on the backbone?
results.context: IID CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, 10 clients, full participation, 100 rounds. Accuracy changes are percentage points versus each architecture’s own FedAvg baseline; encryption time is client-side seconds. No uncertainty is reported.
results.interpretation: Across these reported runs, encryption time spans 2.02–2.12 seconds, while accuracy losses are larger on CIFAR-100 than CIFAR-10.
results.caveat: These are different model baselines, not a ranking of model quality. The table caption mentions only CIFAR-10, but the table itself also contains CIFAR-100; both rows are transcribed here.

evaluation.label: Data and models
evaluation.value: CIFAR-10/100; ResNet-20, MobileNet, ConvNeXt-Tiny, and ConvMixer-256/8 trained from scratch.

evaluation.label: Federated setting
evaluation.value: Flower simulations; principal comparisons use 30 clients, 1 local epoch, 128 clusters, and 20% or 100% participation.

evaluation.label: Compared with
evaluation.value: FedAvg, FedAvg with weight clustering, DeTrust-FL, SEFL, and an EncCluster variant using Huffman coding instead of Binary Fuse filters.

evaluation.label: Privacy evidence
evaluation.value: Arguments for isolation/replay resistance and a cluster-reconstruction experiment measuring embedding MSE; no differential-privacy budget or general inference-attack bound.

limitations: The preprint assumes an honest-but-curious server and setup authority, secure channels, and protected key provisioning. Colluding clients may disclose weights but do not poison updates; denial-of-service and poisoning are excluded.
Binary Fuse filters are not encryption and the paper explicitly disclaims equivalent cryptographic guarantees. Their reconstruction errors are not an established differential-privacy guarantee.

With all other clients colluding, the aggregate can reveal a target’s clustered contribution. Lossy compression prevents exact recovery of original weights but does not establish absence of sensitive information leakage.
Evaluation uses two small vision datasets and reports client encryption time and upstream volume. It does not establish wall-clock, energy, server scalability, or deployed edge-device gains.
takeaways: The main efficiency gain comes from reducing the number of values encrypted to the centroid count.
Protecting centroid values and encoding their positions solve different problems; the server is intended to recover the mappings.
The no-filter variant is more compact, so the extra encoding has a visible communication cost that must be weighed against its narrower threat model.
